enmi-luna-assessment:
I see discussions in which the responsibility of the Artificial Flowers themselves and the management of the remaining danger are treated as a single question.

The Florist’s crimes cannot be attributed to an individual who neither knows their own origin nor intends anyone harm. Yet the problem in this case—that individuals were turned to attacks irrespective of their own will—is not of a kind that testimony to their good character can resolve.

If action is to wait until renewed control actually occurs, it is those attacked again who will bear the cost of that confirmation. Theseus has readily understandable reasons for refusing that choice.

I consider that, under certain conditions, killing someone who bears no responsibility for a crime may nonetheless become necessary to secure safety. Nor do I consider that the person’s refusal, by itself, must invariably invalidate such a decision.

I do not, however, consider the current policy of indiscriminate killing sufficiently justified by the explanations made public.

An unknown control mechanism, a danger that confinement cannot prevent, and the absence of any practicable measure other than killing are three different propositions requiring examination. Uncertainty concerning the first cannot simply serve as an answer to the other two.

If killing is also intended to intimidate, one should ask whose behaviour, and which behaviour, it is expected to change. An individual who understands that voluntary surrender still means death has a reason to remain hidden. The possibility that enforcement itself may obstruct the information needed to find them deserves consideration.

To demand action against a danger does not require treating the lives lost in doing so as having been worthless from the outset.
